newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: India tells WTO to stick to trade.
newsitem.headline: India tells WTO to stick to trade.

text.p: India told the World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Monday to stick to its job of regulating global commerce and not dabble in issues that countries should deal with themselves.
"We strongly feel that the WTO should not lose its basic focus on trade," Indian Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah told the opening day of the WTO's first ministerial conference.

"Any attempt by the WTO to overstep the legitimate boundaries of trade and invade the domestic productions systems is bound to create serious problems and raise basic questions about WTO's competence and credibility," he said.
He said among the issues the 128-member WTO should not be involved in were foreign direct investment (FDI) and workers' rights.

"Core labour standards," an issue being pushed at the WTO mainly by the United States, France and Canada, was merely a mask for undermining the competitive advantages developing countries had because their labour was cheaper, he said.
"We do not see any purpose in bringing this subject into the WTO except possibly to use trade measures to enforce labour standards, if not now, then at a future date," Ramaiah said.
"We are of the opinion that trade measures should not be used to address non-trade objectives, however laudable they may be."
The issue belonged with the International Labour Organisation (ILO), which was set up to deal with it, he added.
Ramaiah said India would also resist pressure, mainly from Japan and Canada as well as the 15-member European Union, to use the WTO to liberalise FDI rules.
"We would urge ministers and delegations present here to reflect on whether such a subject falls within the natural boundaries of their multilateral trade relations," he said.

"The investment policy of a country has to take into account a whole host of complex and inter-related matters of national importance -- regional disparities, income inequalities, employment, taxation and social justice," Ramaiah said.
"A uniform multilateral regime on investment, in whichever forum it is developed, is not in the interest of promoting equitable global development," he added.
"This is because it will seriously constrain the freedom of individual countries to prescribe the role they may wish to assign FDI in their national development strategy."
Ramaiah did say, however, that everyone should agree on another major issue looming at the WTO -- transparency in government contracts -- but said India wanted a procedural agreement.
"There can be no difference of view regarding the need for transparency in government purchases," he said.
"I would be interested in dealing with the subject purely as designed towards achieving a procedural agreement providing for transparency," he said.
